content: Separate and dedicated laboratory spaces are required for sample preparation and amplification. One area should be designated for sample preparation, and another for amplification using real-time PCR. If automated sample preparation is preferred, the m2000 sp instrument must be acquired and maintained with regular servicing in the sample preparation area. For reflex testing, the DNA eluate from the RealTime MTB assay can be used with the RealTime MTB RIF/INH assay on the m2000 system. This approach reduces sample processing and inactivation time. The RealTime MTB RIF/INH assay detects resistance to rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH) by identifying mutations in the rpoB gene, katG gene, and inhA promoter region of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) DNA. Resistance results are categorized as negative (R-), detected (R-det), indeterminate (indet), or undetected (below the limit of detection) based on the detection of wild-type and mutant probes. Specific INH resistance-associated mutations may indicate low-level (INH low R) or high-level (INH high R) resistance. A resistance-negative result suggests no detection of targeted resistance-associated mutations, which may correlate with strain sensitivity but does not rule out all potential resistance-conferring mutations. Opportunities for integrating diagnostic connectivity solutions and e-systems should be explored to meet laboratory strengthening targets under the End TB Strategy. Quality assurance systems for Abbott assays align with those of other moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Validation of the RealTime MTB RIF/INH test should include precision and accuracy measurements for drugs targeting all resistance loci, using well-characterized strains with and without known resistance-associated mutations. To prevent contamination, each run on the m2000 rt instrument must include positive and negative controls to ensure validity. Laboratory spaces should be tested for contamination at least monthly, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Training on the Abbott m2000 system is more complex than other centralized TB testing platforms, requiring at least five days of theoretical and practical training. Emphasis should be placed on reagent management and handling, as reagents are stored under different conditions, and DNA extraction and PCR reagents require reconstitution and manual placement in the correct positions in the m2000 sp instrument. These steps are time-consuming and must be performed accurately for successful testing. The BD MAX MDR-TB test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and resistance to rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH) using multiplexed real-time PCR. For MTBC detection, the test targets multicopy genomic elements IS6110 and IS1081, as well as a single-copy genomic target. RIF resistance detection targets the rpoB gene’s resistance-determining region (RRDR), while INH resistance detection targets the inhA promoter region and the katG gene codon 315. The test is performed on the BD MAX platform, which automates DNA extraction and real-time PCR. Results are available within four hours. The World Health Organization (WHO) includes these tests in the moderate-complexity automated NAAT category. For individuals with pulmonary TB symptoms, these tests may be used on respiratory samples to detect TB, RIF resistance, and INH resistance instead of culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). This recommendation is conditional, with moderate certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy. Subgroups considered include adults, people living with HIV, adolescents, and children. Indeterminate results are more likely in children with paucibacillary TB. Extrapulmonary TB and non-sputum sample testing were not considered due to limited data. The BD MAX MDR-TB test procedure involves manual mixing of sputum with BD MAX STR (sample treatment reagent), incubation, and transfer to a BD MAX MDR-TB sample tube. The BD MAX instrument automates sample preparation, including cell lysis, DNA extraction, magnetic bead-based DNA concentration, and real-time PCR. Detection and reporting are automated, using fluorescent probes to identify MTBC DNA, RIF resistance, and INH resistance. Results are digitally reported within four hours. Operational considerations include testing capacity (48 tests per 8-hour workday), sputum storage and testing conditions, and reagent storage temperatures. BD MAX MDR-TB reagents have a shelf life of at least nine months. Quality assurance systems mimic those of other moderate-complexity automated NAATs. New method verifications should use well-characterized M. tuberculosis strains to ensure sensitivity and resistance detection for RIF and INH. Positive and negative controls must be included in each run, and laboratory spaces should be tested for contamination monthly. Training and competency assessment are essential for laboratory staff and clinicians to appropriately review and interpret resistance results for all included medicines.
